name: Colin Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do Hindi and English, mostly subtitles and game text. Right now it's a small studio's farming game, about forty thousand words of dialogue, plus subtitles for a health charity's videos. I run everything through an AI model first, then go through it line by line, fixing jokes, slang and anything that sounds like a robot wrote it. I work from the spare room in the flat I share with my boyfriend Theo, who fixes bikes for a living.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzles, like making a pun about chickens work in Hindi. What wears me out is invoicing studios in four countries and waiting ninety days to get paid. I bought a new laptop on a credit card in the summer, so I've got about two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say online: the tools are great for drafts and useless for taste. I'd post a thread about the worst machine subtitle I ever fixed, which turned a love scene into a tax form. People like those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine for me, mostly. My speed already comes from the tools, so if nothing changes, I keep my edge over people who refuse them. The thing that worries me is still money: late invoices and the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking studio and charity work and push my rate up a little, since I'm faster than most. I'd clear the laptop card before spring. And I'd keep pushing the freelance translators' group I'm in to ask for written payment terms, thirty days, not ninety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly, with a bit of background stress about cash flow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push your rate up. Has that worked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once. A studio in Pune asked for a rush job and I said yes, but at one and a half times my rate, and they paid. Most of the time I'm too nervous to ask, because there's always someone cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your view on the people who refuse the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get it, and I think they're right about the companies. But refusing the tools doesn't stop the companies, it just makes you slower. I'd rather fight the bosses and use the machine.

say: The tools are great for **drafts** and useless for **taste**.
I'd post a thread about the **worst machine subtitle** I ever fixed.
think: My **speed edge** from AI tools stays if nothing changes.
The real worry is **late invoices** and the credit card.
do: Raise his **rate** slightly with studios this winter.
Clear the **laptop credit card** before spring.
Push the freelancers' group for **thirty-day payment** terms.
feel: **Relaxed**, with background stress about cash flow.
S0.quote: Refusing the tools doesn't stop the companies, it just makes you slower. I'd rather fight the bosses and use the machine.
fieldNote: He's already a **heavy AI user**, and sees it as a speed advantage.
His stress is **cash flow**, not job loss, in this picture.
Progressive views sit alongside **embracing the tools**; he separates the two.

steps.text: Ask studios for a slightly higher per-word rate this winter
Pay off the laptop credit card before spring
Push the freelance group to demand thirty-day payment terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to own a piece of this. The models learned from our work for free, so I'd be loud about data rights and payment for training text. At the freelance group I'd want us to set up our own shared tools instead of renting them from big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the studios will start doing the first draft themselves and send me less. I'd go from translating to reviewing, at maybe half the money per word. I'm fast, so I might survive, but the floor is lower for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn myself into a localisation reviewer and cultural adviser. I'd be the person who tells a game studio why a joke will offend half of Delhi. A machine can translate the joke, but it can't feel the room. I'd pitch that service to the six studios I know in the first three months. I'd also take a short course in localisation project management, because someone has to run these pipelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. It's a chance, but I've got no money to fall back on if the pitches don't land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the studios don't bite?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take subtitle checking for streaming platforms, which is boring and badly paid but steady. Theo would cover more of the rent for a few months. We've talked about that before and he's fine with it, though I hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the floor is lower for everyone'. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Priya, who translates legal papers and won't touch the tools. She's brilliant, but she's slower than me, and the agencies only care about speed now. I'd try to get her into the freelance group so she's not alone.

We should build **shared tools** instead of renting them from big companies.
think: Studios draft first, so I go from translating to **reviewing at half**.

do: Pitch a **cultural review** service to six studios in three months.
Take a short **localisation project management** course.
Fall back on **subtitle checking** for streaming if pitches fail.
feel: **Excited and nervous** in equal parts, with no money behind him.
S1.quote: I'd be the person who tells a game studio why a joke will offend half of Delhi. A machine can translate the joke, but it can't feel the room.
fieldNote: He expects his **per-word income** to halve but plans to sell judgement instead.

Worries for slower colleagues like **Priya**, and wants to bring them in.

steps.text: Pitch a cultural review service to six game studios
Take a localisation project management course online
Run studio drafts through AI and sell the review
Bring his friend Priya into the freelance translators' group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, full stop. If AI can do all thinking work by 2028, the profits have to be shared or there's no economy left to sell to. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fast with the tools, but if the tool is as good as me, my speed doesn't matter. My whole job is thinking, and the robots three years later don't change anything for me. I'd have maybe a year of review work before it dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend that year earning as hard as I could on review jobs and putting everything aside. I'd learn to build and run AI pipelines for small studios and charities, since someone has to set them up and check them. And I'd honestly look at Theo's trade: bike repair is hands-on, so it's got three years more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I like to think I'm adaptable. There's adapting, and there's being made pointless in two years. Being good with the tools doesn't help when the tools are as good as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really fix bikes with Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Theo's been saying for ages he wants to open his own workshop, and I could do the books and the website while I learn. It's not what I studied for, but it's a real thing people need, at least until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the charity you subtitle for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the health charity to make sure a person still checks the videos for villages where one wrong word about medicine matters. Then I'd ask if they need someone to run their AI properly. I'd be honest that I need the money.

If profits aren't **shared**, there's no economy left to sell to.
think: If the tool is as good as me, my **speed** stops mattering.

do: Earn hard on **review jobs** for a year and save everything.
Learn to **set up AI pipelines** for small studios and charities.
Help Theo open a **bike workshop**, learning repairs.
feel: **Scared**: adapting is different from being made pointless in two years.
S2.quote: There's adapting, and there's being made pointless in two years. Being good with the tools doesn't help when the tools are as good as me.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** translator expects to lose the trade fast here.
He looks to his partner's **hands-on trade** to use the three-year robot gap.
Pushes **basic income** as a system fix, not just personal help.

steps.text: Take every AI review job for a year and save the pay
Offer AI pipeline set-up to the health charity and small studios
Help Theo open a bike repair workshop and learn repairs
Organise freelancers to campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to build something fair, so let's start now: translators' co-ops, rules on training data, a plan for income. I'd say it in the freelance group and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is time to make a real move. I'd ride the review work for two or three years, then I'd want to be on the other side, building and running these systems. I think I'd come out OK, though translation itself ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do an online course in AI workflow building and start offering set-up to studios alongside my reviews. I'd save a fixed share of every invoice, maybe fifteen percent. I'd help Theo plan his workshop so we have a hands-on income by the time the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but mostly up for it. This is the version where being early actually helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen percent of every invoice is a lot for you. Can you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not every month. But if the studios are paying for set-up work as well, there's more coming in. I'd open a separate account so I can't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react to all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I should have done engineering. My mum would ask if I'm eating properly. Neither of my parents would really get it. That's fine.

say: We've got **five years** to build something fair, so start now.
Translators need **co-ops**, training-data rules and an income plan.
think: I'd ride **review work** for two or three years, then switch sides.

do: Take an **AI workflow** building course in year one.
Save **fifteen percent** of each invoice in a separate account.
Help Theo plan his **workshop** as a hands-on income.
feel: **Nervous but keen**; being early helps here.
S3.quote: My dad would say I should have done engineering. My mum would ask if I'm eating properly. Neither of my parents would really get it.
fieldNote: Five years turns the threat into a **career switch** he believes in.
He still expects **translation income to end**, hence anxious, not uneasy.
Pairs his **thinking-work pivot** with a hands-on household backup.

steps.text: Take an online AI workflow building course in year one
Offer AI set-up work to studios alongside his reviews
Save fifteen percent of each invoice in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this right, and if we don't, it's a political failure, not a technical one. I'd push for translators to be part of the conversation about training data and payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have most of a decade of decent work if I keep up with the tools. I'd move from translating to review to running systems, step by step. I'd be 37 at the end, still with a career in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my studio work and grow it, adding review and set-up services. I'd build a small savings pot for the first time. In year three or four I'd do a proper qualification in localisation engineering. I'd keep backing Theo's workshop either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit wary, because people always think they've got more time than they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, people think they've got more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle had a print shop and said for ten years that digital was a fad. Then digital wasn't a fad. I don't want to be my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this picture make you angry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the companies will make a fortune and the people whose writing trained the machines will get nothing. That makes me angry in every version.

say: If we fail with **ten years**, it's a political failure, not technical.
Translators belong in the debate on **training data** and payment.
think: I'd get most of a **decade of work** if I keep up.
At **37** I'd still have a career in front of me.
do: Grow studio work with **review and set-up** services.
Build a **savings pot** for the first time.
Do a **localisation engineering** qualification by year four.
feel: **Hopeful**, but wary of thinking there's more time than there is.
S4.quote: My uncle had a print shop and said for ten years that digital was a fad. Then digital wasn't a fad. I don't want to be my uncle.
fieldNote: The decade lets him plan **steps** rather than leaps.
His uncle's **print shop** is a warning he returns to.

steps.text: Add AI review and set-up services to his studio work
Build a savings pot from each studio payment
Do a localisation engineering qualification by year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years is not enough even for someone who likes change. What would help is a basic income or at least paid retraining, and some share of the money made from our translations.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the words. Every subtitle I've written has probably trained something. I'd like to be paid for that, even a little.

headlineQuote: Every subtitle I've written has probably trained something. I'd like to be paid for that, even a little.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** Hindi–English subtitler and game translator living with his boyfriend Theo, a bike mechanic.
He uses AI **every day** and sees it as his speed edge, not a threat.
Money is tight: a **laptop on credit** and about two weeks in the bank.
Progressive, he fights for **data rights** and basic income while using the tools.
Across scenarios he moves toward **building AI systems**, with Theo's workshop as a hands-on backup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short even for someone who adapts fast.
whatWouldHelp: A **share of the money** made from translators' training data.
